idiom_name: explicit release contract: *_release() hands the resource back to its owner (one cleanup label or __attribute__((cleanup)))
implementation_notes: C has no destructors and no way to put ownership into a type, so the hand-back is an API contract: the factory or pool returns a handle whose one documented release function gives it back to the owner, while the owner keeps a separate destroy path the borrower never calls. Funnel every exit path through a single cleanup label, and let the compiler run the call where it helps - GCC/Clang's __attribute__((cleanup(fn))) runs a function when a variable goes out of scope, which automates the timing but not the ownership decision. The classic wrapper structure makes sense only as a hand-written struct-plus-release pair when the same handle crosses many call sites; otherwise the disciplined cleanup label is the honest realization.
pitfalls: Release and destroy are separate functions with no type difference (pool_return vs conn_close); calling the wrong one on a borrowed handle either leaks a pool slot or frees a connection the pool still tracks.
A rejected checkout leaves the handle null or uninitialised while the cleanup function still runs at scope exit - the cleanup must tolerate an empty guard, or every failure path releases garbage.

__attribute__((cleanup)) is a GCC/Clang extension: it runs on scope exit including early return, so declaring the guard after an early return, or copying the raw pointer out of the guard, silently drops the hand-back.
